benchmark: Zipling app against rival apps and tools, for the published benchmark

machine.chip: Apple M1 Pro, 10 cores (8 performance, 2 efficiency)
machine.storage: internal Apple SSD, 1 TB (sets read from and archives written to the same APFS volume)

zipling.engine: Arca, archive format 3, locked presets of 2026-10-31
zipling.how: the installed /Applications/Zipling.app, driven through its AppleScript compress and extract commands; the row's time is the app's own clock (its timing log, from the command's arrival in the app to the finished file; make_s_app); the AppleScript wall time minus a measured no-work round trip (make_s_osa) and the raw wall time (make_s_raw) are kept beside it; CPU and peak footprint of the app process sampled through proc_pid_rusage

zipgeist.how: the installed app, driven through its Finder menu (Compress As > Options), the only way it compresses; timed by a stopwatch from the click on Compress to the last busy moment of its processes, with the archive's write time as a floor; six settings: ZIP Fast, ZIP Normal, tar.zst Fast, 7z Normal, 7z Best, tar.xz Best

finder.how: Finder's Compress command and double-click to expand (Archive Utility), timed by the same stopwatch on Archive Utility's processes; also ditto -c -k --sequesterRsrc --keepParent / ditto -x -k from the command line, which is the same engine (finder-zip rows)

7zip.how: 7zz a -t7z -mx=5 (Normal) and -mx=9 (Ultra), symbolic links kept (-snl); extract with -snld20. Stands in for Keka and BetterZip, which use 7-Zip's code; neither has its own engine

winrar.version: RAR 7.23 for macOS (command line; WinRAR has no Mac app)
winrar.how: rar a -m1 (Fastest), -m3 (Normal, its default), -m5 -s (Best, solid); links kept (-ol); all cores

zstd.version: 1.5.7 (Homebrew; the second pass, results-2026-10-31-apps-zx.jsonl, which the report and the website use). The main run's rows are zstd 1.5.6 from a conda environment that sat first in the harness's PATH

xz.version: XZ Utils 5.8.4 (Homebrew; the second pass, results-2026-10-31-apps-zx.jsonl, which the report and the website use). The main run's rows are XZ Utils 5.6.4 from the same conda environment

method: Every tool runs on every set twice, the second round in reverse order; the better of the two rounds counts; the first round's extracted tree is compared with the source byte for byte (names, types, bytes, link targets).
Each set is read once (tar to /dev/null) before its runs, so every tool starts with the files in the page cache.

A set's runs start only when the 1-minute load is under 2.5 (the Mac otherwise idle), waiting up to ten minutes. In the main run the last two sets (disk images, third-party apps) went on after the wait at 3.7: an animated wallpaper and a background app kept the idle load there; their rows match the quiet engine run of the same presets within noise.

Zipling and the command-line rivals alternate within a set (bench/research/apprun.py). The main run (phase 3) ran unattended from 00:05 to 02:32 on 1 November 2026; the log's clock jumps back an hour between the disk images and the third-party apps because daylight saving time ended at 02:00.

zstd and xz were measured twice: the main run picked up zstd 1.5.6 and XZ Utils 5.6.4 from a conda environment first in the harness's PATH; a second pass of the same four settings on all nine sets with the Homebrew releases (zstd 1.5.7, XZ Utils 5.8.4; APPRUN_LOAD=4, same night) replaces those rows in the report and on the website. The first-pass rows stay in the main file for the record.

Zipgeist and Finder's Compress need the screen: they ran under full-screen control, which keeps WindowServer and the Claude app at about one core together; one Zipling Fast run per set in the same session (arca-fast-clock) shows the effect on the clock.

A row is won when Zipling is smaller, faster to make and faster to extract at once; 1:1 by level (Fast against the fast settings, Default against the normal ones, Max and Ultra against the best), upsets listed separately (bench/research/levels.py).
